structure.title: Books I–IV · Follow an empire as it spreads
structure.text: The question of conflict between Greeks and non-Greeks leads first to Croesus of Lydia and then eastwards with the Persian kings. Each new conquest is an occasion to meet the people whose land an imperial account might reduce to a name.

structure.title: Books V–VI · Revolt brings the mainland within reach
structure.text: An uprising in the Greek cities of Asia Minor draws other cities into a war whose consequences travel farther than its instigators intend. The road to Marathon runs through appeals for help, refusals and dangerous promises.

structure.title: Books VII–IX · Armies are assembled one decision at a time
structure.text: The invasion under Xerxes brings processions, speeches, arguments over oracles and disputes among allies into the same narrative. Herodotus can stop before a famous encounter to ask who knew which road, or whose advice nearly prevailed.

people.name: Croesus
people.role: A rich king who needs an interpreter
people.text: The king can afford gifts for oracles and furnish his court with every visible advantage. He still has to decide what an answer means. His story establishes how easily prosperity can masquerade as understanding.

people.name: Herodotus
people.role: Investigator and collector of rival accounts
people.text: Sometimes he has seen the thing described. Elsewhere he reports what priests, travellers or local communities say. When two accounts survive side by side, their disagreement tells us something about the work of recovering an event.

context.title: The apparent detours
context.text: A river's course, a burial custom or a story about a king can interrupt a campaign for pages. Such passages preserve a local way of understanding the world just when an army is about to enter it.

notice.text: Listen for the interpreter inside the oracle.
notice.why: An ambiguous answer can sound astonishingly precise to someone who desperately wants permission. The chain of interpretation is often where responsibility for a decision becomes visible.

notice.text: Watch a map become an argument.
notice.why: Distances and routes look different to a recruiter seeking allies, a king planning an invasion and a community on the march's path. Geography can change a listener's mind as decisively as a speech.

opening: Croesus has wealth, power, and an oracle whose answer seems to promise victory. He goes to war and discovers that a prophecy can be perfectly accurate while meaning something other than he hoped. Herodotus collects such failures of understanding as he investigates how Greeks and Persians came to fight. Kings, travellers, priests, and rival witnesses supply his material. The result has the curiosity of someone who cannot pass a good story, and the seriousness of someone asking how entire peoples become enemies.
